analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act in full and replaces it with tax deductions, high-risk pool funding, and looser insurance rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to eight House committees but never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and its companion reconciliation law as if they had never passed, wiping out protections for people with preexisting conditions, the Medicaid expansion, and the subsidized marketplace. In their place it would make medical expenses fully tax-deductible with no income threshold, fund state high-risk pools with $5 billion a year for five years, and let insurers sell individual policies into any state under the rules of whichever state they pick, escaping most consumer-protection laws of the state where the buyer lives. It would also create federally certified association health plans that small employers could join, exempted from most state insurance regulation.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers gain a new multistate selling freedom, because they could designate one state as their 'primary state' and sell into every other state largely under that state's laws, free from the secondary state's coverage mandates and rate rules. Wealthier households who itemize gain from an unlimited medical expense deduction, which only helps taxpayers who itemize and whose medical costs are a meaningful share of income. Trade associations and chambers of commerce gain a new role sponsoring health plans, and small employers would get another coverage option.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would let a healthy buyer purchase cheaper individual coverage approved in a state with fewer coverage mandates, and would forbid insurers from raising that individual's renewal premium based on health status once the policy is issued [S3].

It would fund state high-risk pools at $5 billion per year for fiscal 2011 through 2015, giving people who cannot buy coverage on the open market a place to go once the ACA's guaranteed-issue rules were repealed [S2] [S3].
It would allow the full deduction of medical expenses with no percentage-of-income threshold, reducing taxes for people with large out-of-pocket medical costs who itemize [S2] [S3].
It would let small employers join association health plans certified under federal law, pooling together to buy coverage the way larger groups do [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the people who gained coverage and protections under the Affordable Care Act would pay: those with preexisting conditions would rely on high-risk pools that historically charged high premiums and enrolled only a fraction of eligible people; people newly eligible for Medicaid or for marketplace subsidies would lose that help; and buyers of out-of-state policies would give up the consumer-protection and benefit-mandate laws of their own state, since the selling insurer's chosen state's laws would govern. The federal treasury would also absorb the cost of the new deduction and the high-risk pool funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and subsidized coverage

drawbacks.text: Repealing the ACA would end guaranteed issue and the ban on preexisting-condition denials for the individual market, leaving people who are already sick dependent on high-risk pools; before the ACA, state high-risk pools typically charged premiums well above standard rates and enrolled far fewer people than would have qualified [S2] [S3].

The out-of-state selling provision would let an insurer pick the state with the weakest rules and sell into every other state, exempting it from the secondary state's coverage mandates and rate-change restrictions; the bill's own required disclosure notice tells buyers the policy 'may be less expensive... because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws' of their state [S3].

The unlimited medical-expense deduction helps only taxpayers who itemize, which skews toward higher-income households, and combined with the loss of ACA-related revenue it would add to federal deficits [S2].

Association health plans have a documented history of insolvency and fraud when exempted from state oversight; this bill responds with federal certification, reserve requirements, stop-loss insurance, and a federal backstop fund, but the solvency safeguards add administrative weight and do not eliminate the risk that a plan fails and participants are left with unpaid claims [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real price relief to a specific group: healthy buyers of individual insurance, who could buy leaner policies approved under another state's rules, plus a fully deductible medical-expense break. The cost falls on the other end of the risk pool. Repealing the ACA without a working replacement for guaranteed issue means people with preexisting conditions are thrown back onto high-risk pools, whose record of high premiums and limited enrollment is the reason the ACA's drafters moved away from them. The cross-state selling provision, the bill's signature idea, works largely by letting insurers escape the consumer-protection laws of the buyer's own state — the savings come from the buyer accepting weaker coverage, not from anyone else absorbing the cost. On balance the bill's gains are concentrated and its costs are broad and fall on people who are already sick or economically vulnerable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to eight House committees, one subcommittee looked at it, and then nothing happened for two years until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Broun of Georgia introduced the bill on January 18, 2011 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to eight House committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Appropriations, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, and Rules [S5].

In January and February 2011 it was referred to a Natural Resources subcommittee on Indian and Alaska Native Affairs and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, the only subcommittee activity on record [S5].

Only one Republican cosponsor joined the bill, and no committee ever held a markup or reported it; the record of actions ends there and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4] [S5] [S1].

The House Republican leadership pursued ACA repeal through a different vehicle: a separate full-repeal bill (H.R. 2) that the House passed on January 19, 2011, the day after this bill was introduced; that measure passed the House but died in the Democratic-controlled Senate, and President Obama said he would veto any repeal.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, people who relied on the Affordable Care Act — those with preexisting conditions, Medicaid expansion enrollees, and marketplace subsidy recipients — kept those protections for the rest of the Congress. Insurers did not gain the cross-state selling exemption, and higher-income taxpayers did not get the unlimited deduction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People with preexisting conditions kept ACA protections

sides.party_line_note: ACA repeal split by party — the House's separate repeal bill passed with no Democratic support — but this particular bill drew only one cosponsor beyond Rep. Broun [S4], suggesting the party leadership never rallied behind it.

industries.note: The bill would let an insurer designate one state as its primary state and sell individual policies into all 50 states under that state's laws, exempting it from the buyer's own state's coverage mandates and rate restrictions. The gain comes from selling leaner, less-regulated policies; the bill's own disclosure notice warns buyers the policy may skip services their state mandates.

Removing the 7.5%-of-income threshold makes all medical expenses deductible, but only taxpayers who itemize benefit, which skews toward higher-income households. The revenue cost is spread across all federal taxpayers.

industries.industry: Trade associations and chambers of commerce
industries.note: The bill creates a federal certification for association health plans, giving associations a new role pooling small employers' coverage. Workers could gain a cheaper group option, but plans largely escape state insurance regulation, and the federal solvency rules and backstop fund exist precisely because such plans have failed before.

Both the cross-state selling provision and the association health plan title preempt most state insurance rules, shrinking state regulators' authority over policies sold to their residents, though states keep narrow powers over solvency, fraud, and claims practices.

Repealing the ACA ends guaranteed issue and preexisting-condition protections; the bill's answer is $5 billion a year for state high-risk pools through 2015, a mechanism that historically charged high premiums and enrolled only a fraction of eligible people.
